messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 48
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Rabbi
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 41

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds, Being Watched: Feeling watched or observed, Media / News: Related news
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others, Avoid Sex: Sex, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next, No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ruth had been a rabbi for fifteen years when the community center was bombed. She remembered the sound before she remembered anything else—a crack that split the air and then a roar that seemed to come from inside her own chest. She had been in the kitchen, preparing tea for the evening adult education class, and when the wall came down she had crawled through debris toward the voices. She pulled two people out before the firefighters arrived. For weeks afterward, the local news played the footage of her, hands bleeding, coat covered in dust, helping the wounded into ambulances. People called her a hero. Ruth could not look at the footage. Every time she saw herself on the screen, she felt a cold sickness in her stomach, because what she saw was not a hero. What she saw was someone who had not done enough. Someone who had been in the kitchen making tea while people died.

The guilt had not faded with time. It had calcified. She would never forgive herself for not doing more, she told her husband David one night, and he had taken her hands and said, “You saved lives, Ruth. You saved two people.” But she could not hear it. Even when others told her she was safe, she found it impossible to believe. The world had shown her what it was capable of, and she had learned the lesson permanently: nothing good could happen to her anymore. She had come to believe that her life had peaked before the explosion, and everything after was just aftermath.

She had stopped having sex with David about four months after the bombing. It was not something she had decided consciously. It was more that she could not bear the vulnerability of it—the way her body became soft and open, the way she could not watch the door while her eyes were closed. She had not explained this to David. She had simply become tired at night, or had a headache, or needed to finish work. He had stopped asking eventually, and she was grateful, and also ashamed of her gratitude.

Her days had become a constant, exhausting vigilance. She scanned every room she entered, noting exits, assessing the weight of furniture, the thickness of walls. She checked her surroundings for signs of danger the way other people checked the weather—automatically, habitually, without deciding to do it. At night it was worse. She found it harder to feel safe after dark, even in her own home. She lay awake listening to the creak of the house, the distant sound of a car door, the rustle of trees. Every bang—a dropped book, a slammed cabinet, a firework two blocks away—sent her heart into her throat. She had become a person who startled at normal sounds, and she hated that about herself.

Her work as a rabbi had become difficult in ways she had not anticipated. She could no longer lead the evening classes, because the community center had been rebuilt and the new building looked almost exactly like the old one, and the smell of the carpet reminded her of dust and blood. She had delegated those classes to a younger colleague. She avoided the news entirely. When well-meaning congregants brought up the anniversary of the bombing, or mentioned her bravery, she changed the subject or found a reason to leave the room. She did not want to be reminded. She did not want anyone to see her as a survivor, because survivors were people who had moved on, and she had not moved on.

She had come to feel watched. Not by anyone specific—not by a person or a group—but by something. The feeling was constant, a prickling at the back of her neck, a sense that she was being observed and judged. She found herself checking over her shoulder in the grocery store, scanning the faces in the congregation during Shabbat services, looking for someone who might be watching her. She knew it did not make sense. She knew the bomber was dead. But knowing something and believing it were two different things, and she had stopped believing in safety a long time ago.

What had finally brought her to seek help was not the fear or the guilt or the sleeplessness, though all of those were present. It was a moment in the grocery store, six weeks ago, when a cart had clattered to the floor in the next aisle and she had dropped to her knees, hands over her head, in front of a display of canned tomatoes. A stranger had touched her shoulder and asked if she was okay, and Ruth had looked up at the fluorescent lights and the cheerful produce signs and thought: I cannot live like this anymore. She had made an appointment the next morning.

She was afraid of what therapy might ask her to do. She was afraid of revisiting the moment she had worked so hard to avoid. But she was also afraid of staying exactly where she was, scanning every room for a threat that might not come, waiting for nothing good to happen, feeling watched by a world she no longer trusted. She did not know if she could get better. She was not sure she deserved to. But she had come, and she was sitting in the chair, and that was something.
